public_rationale: The amendment chronology identifies July 3, 2024 as the latest amendment before August 10 [e3]. Foley's July 9 analysis of that version describes reasonable safeguards, protocols providing reasonable assurance, and release restrictions where an unreasonable risk of critical harm remains [e1]. These qualified standards support the claim when “not to fully mitigate” means not guaranteeing elimination of every possibility of harm [e1]. Foley also lists assessment, certification and reporting duties, so this finding does not mean safeguards were the only obligations [e1].
limitations: The complete July 3 statutory text was not directly verified; the finding relies on contemporaneous legal analysis.
The earlier committee analysis explicitly distinguishes reasonable assurance from certainty, but addresses the June 20 text rather than independently establishing the July 3 requirements [e2].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: SB-1047 requires developers only to implement reasonable safeguards against critical harms, not to fully mitigate them.

statement.excerpt: Even then developers are required only to implement "reasonable safeguards" against these severe risks--not to fully mitigate them.
statement.document_title: An open letter to Fei-Fei Li concerning California’s proposed AI regulation, SB-1047

our_interpretation: Read 'not to fully mitigate' as not requiring elimination of every possibility of critical harm.
In context, 'only' contrasts reasonable risk reduction with complete prevention; it does not deny separate testing, reporting, certification or other procedural duties.
Use the July 3 amendment, the latest published version before the August 10 post.
criteria.support_condition: The applicable safeguards and release standards require reasonable precautions against critical harms and unreasonable risks, without guaranteeing zero residual risk.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The applicable provisions require complete elimination of critical-harm risk despite reasonable precautions, or impose an unqualified guarantee that such harm cannot occur.
